#9799. Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

An attacker could write arbitrary files and read sensitive files via images uploaded to the Rails Active Storage ImageMagick integration, possibly positioning a threat actor for lateral movement.

A critical vulnerability in Rails could send impacted Web servers off the tracks.

Rails, or Ruby on Rails, is a Web application framework built on Ruby. The framework's Active Storage component handles file uploads and can use the ImageMagick image processing suite to analyze uploaded images. Unfortunately, a flaw enables attackers to write arbitrary files to a Web server via ImageMagick.

The vulnerability (which is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9) is critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and is considered so severe because an attacker could upload a crafted image file to write arbitrary files, read sensitive files, and access secrets such as secret_key_base files, external system credentials, database passwords, and third-party tokens. These secrets could then be used for lateral movement or remote code execution into external systems.

As a GitHub advisory published by the Rails maintainers explains, "A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process."

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

The vulnerability exists because ImageMagick doesn't necessarily decide how to process a file (i.e., which coder it uses) based on the filename or extension, but rather on its contents. This means an attacker can upload an image file named "maliciousfile.jpeg" that contains content that causes ImageMagick to invoke a different coder. This can potentially allow arbitrary file reads or writes on the server.

Vulnerable versions of Active Storage include those 8.0 versions prior to 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 versions prior to 8.1.4.1. Those affected organizations running Rails applications that use ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing run with a security policy that does not block the affected coders, and accept uploads from untrusted users.

Active Storage patches are available now. The GitHub page includes further mitigation requirements for applications that use MiniMagick and ImageMagick.

Additionally, if an application stores attachments through the Disk service, users should "change secret_key_base and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens," the GitHub advisory said. Users should not retain exposed secrets as a fallback.

If a user requires a workaround, the GitHub page offers system rules the user can apply into ImageMagick's system policy.

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for exposure management vendor watchTowr, tells Dark Reading the firm has already reproduced the vulnerability in a lab environment, and "that against the right target, exploitation won't be difficult at all."

Moreover, he says he'd be surprised if public proof-of-concept exploit code took more than a few days to come to light.

"For attackers, reproducing the vulnerability here is likely the easy part, as the patterns and primitives involved in exploitation are well established," Knott says. "The hard part is finding software and deployments that are common enough, and configured in a vulnerable way, to deliver impact at scale indiscriminately."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9798. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9797. FreeBSD GUS

FreeBSD has a pretty neat safe memory reclamation scheme (something akin to RCU), that's also been adopted by XNU that hasn't really been well-documented outside of code comments, and I thought it would've been interesting to write about it.

The problem of safe memory reclamation (SMR) shows up notably when working with lock-free data structures. Lock-free data structures are the bread and butter of modern scalability in operating systems, and they often allow much higher throughput than their finely grained locked counterparts, but they come with their own issues.

Lock-free data structure code in unmanaged languages needs to carefully manage the liveness of the objects it manages, i.e it must guarantee that memory is freed if and only if no one is able to access it. This arises because there is no synchronization around the access of the data structure, so an object that is removed can still be visible concurrently by another CPU (who might have made a local copy).

More broadly, SMR schemes can also be used for other things than memory reclamation, I like to think of them as providing barriers ensuring that all participants (read: CPUs or threads) have passed through a certain point.

SMR schemes broadly fall in two families: Epoch-based reclamation (EBR) and Quiescent-state based reclamation (QSBR). You might have also heard of Hazard Pointers (HP), which are useful on their own but are seldom seen in operating systems (at least, that I know of!).

QSBR is notable because you might've heard of it called a different name by the Linux project, RCU (Read-Copy-Update)! RCU's author, Paul McKenney, actually invented QSBR for the DYNIX operating system.

RCU has been described extensively, and I would recommend reading McKenney's excellent LWN Articles to learn more. The TL;DR is that there are three operations: rcu_read_lock, rcu_read_unlock and rcu_synchronize, the read operations are used to guard reads around potentially-freed memory (i.e to enter a read section) and the synchronize function waits until there is no CPU in a read section (this could be used to wait until memory is safe to be freed).

The gist of the algorithm is that memory is known to be safe to free when all CPUs have gone through at least one quiescent point ever since the object was removed from its data structure (a grace period), and read section operations block those quiescent points from ever happening.

In practice, this can be implemented by having a quiescent point on context switches and inhibiting preemption during read operations. The core of the algorithm is actually pretty simple, and much of the complexity of the Linux code stems from making this scalable (Tree RCU) and handling other RCU flavors (e.g preemptible RCU).

FreeBSD's safe memory reclamation scheme is called GUS and is part of the EBR family.

Epoch-based reclamation was first described by Keir Fraser in his now-famous thesis titled Practical Lock-freedom (link). The way it works is that there is a global epoch which moves through 0, 1 and 2. When a thread enters a read section, it pins itself by reading the global epoch and copying it into its local slot.

When a writer retires an object, it goes into a "limbo" bag tagged with the current epoch (really, the epoch is used as an index into an array of three linked lists). The global epoch is advanced by polling all other threads and checking whether or not they have acknowledged the current epoch by reading their local slot; if it so happens that they have, then the global epoch is advanced and memory that was retired two epochs ago can now be freed.

It is now time to reveal that GUS really means Global Unbounded Sequences, and it tackles on issue #1 by making epochs unbounded (hence the name) and issue #2 is somewhat mitigated by clever integration with the broader system.

I am using sequence and epoch interchangeably here. Confusing, I know!

The way GUS works is that there is a global, monotonically increasing write sequence, as well as a global read sequence, which represents the last minimum observed sequence across CPUs.

Each CPU also keeps track of its own local sequence when it is pinned, akin to how EBR does things.

The algorithm goes as follows, in pseudocode:

I will not go too much into details about the atomic operations here, if you're curious, they have been extensively described by people smarter than me! The basic idea, however, is that one needs to remember that all operations after enter must not be reordered w.r.t the publication of the epoch (the store to cur_seq)

The basic idea is therefore that a sequence is essentially a timestamp[1], and that the read sequence is always playing catch-up with the write sequence, but never actually reaching it, (i.e there is always at least a separation of 1 between both). Obviously, in practice, there is a bit more to it especially w.r.t memory orderings, but the whole thing is still freakishingly simple and can be implemented in a few hundred lines, see the FreeBSD implementation here.

The unbounded epochs solved the issue #1 that was presented earlier, but what about issue #2: how is polling amortized?

Jeff Roberson, the author of GUS, also wrote the UMA (universal memory allocator) implementation, and both tie nicely together.

To me, the way GUS is integrated with the allocator is really its distinguishing feature and what makes the whole thing work well.

The UMA allocator is essentially a modernized slab allocator, which was first implemented in Solaris and described in Jeff Bonwick's influential papers[2][3] in the early 2000s. To make things scale on SMP systems, it relies on per-CPU "buckets" (magazines in Bonwickspeak), which are essentially an array of N objects on which objects are popped from and pushed onto quickly. A certain amount of pre-allocated buckets are stored in a per-zone (kmem_cache in Bonwickspeak) "depot" from which empty buckets and full buckets are pulled. N, i.e the size of buckets, is dynamically resized according to measured contention on the depot lock; high contention needs to be reduced by increasing the bucket size, which provides amortization over the (potentially) slow and contended operation of going to the depot.

GUS and the allocator join together by allowing the creation of "SMR zones" which are zones that do careful handling around the freeing of objects. Someone wanting to write a lock-free data structure could create a SMR zone for their object and do allocations and frees effectively transparently.

On SMR zones, when the allocator notices a bucket is completely free (i.e full of objects), it advances the write sequence and stamps the bucket with it, then puts it back at the end of the depot free list.

When the allocator then needs to get a free bucket from the depot, it gets the bucket from the head of the free list, and then polls other CPUs for the sequence that is stamped on that bucket. If the goal has already been reached, then the bucket can be reused, otherwise, the allocator will fallback on allocating another bucket itself.

What's cool about this is that buckets naturally provide amortization for those SMR operations; polling is done on a batch of objects at once, and not on a per-object basis (which avoids starting one write sequence per object) and growing the buckets lengthens the time spent before touching the depot again, which gives the time for other buckets to age.

Remember that the GUS algorithm relies on finding the lowest sequence across all CPUs, which means that oftentimes, if buckets are aged as expected, then a single poll operation could allow the reuse of many buckets at the same time, e.g if the depot free list contains buckets stamped with 100, 101, 102 and we notice via polling that the new minimum sequence is 103, then all of those buckets can be reused immediately, which avoids having to do future polls for those buckets.

That is what makes everything click together and the polling not so bad anymore!

Apple's XNU has also adopted a very similar scheme but with many goodies on top. For instance, they support preemptible read sections and a call_rcu-style API. The way it integrates with their zone allocator, however, is quite interesting and its implementation differs enough that I deem it worthy to be described here as well.

XNU's zone allocator (zalloc) is, like UMA, also essentially a modernized slab allocator; I will not try to explain it in depth here because it is quite sophisticated (over 10k lines!), and I am keeping this in reserve for another post, but I will go over the details of how their buckets are reused.

What's interesting is that zalloc does not rely on resizing buckets at all, instead, buckets are kept at a fixed size (something like 8 objects), and a per-CPU depot is installed on top of the per-zone depot, which they call the "recirculation depot" (this should make sense later why such a name was used). This per-CPU depot is then resized with an algorithm similar to the one used to resize buckets, providing the same kind of amortization.

When a bucket becomes full and ready to be recycled, it is stamped with a deferred advance of the write sequence and put onto the per-CPU depot. When allocation is in need of a bucket, it polls the head of the per-CPU depot, and grabs it if it has expired. Otherwise, it does four things:

Since the head of the per-CPU depot hasn't expired yet, this means that all buckets that sit in the per-CPU depot are not yet ready. All buckets are therefore put at the end of the zone depot, as to let them age behind the buckets that were already in depot.

The last bucket in the depot is the newest, its sequence is taken and the global write sequence is advanced to that one immediately, this allows to do one write sequence write for many buckets.

A batch of buckets is then pulled from the head of the zone depot, these are the oldest buckets, so they are more likely to have expired. The batching here avoids having to constantly thrash on the depot and avoids contention on it.

Finally, the oldest bucket we just freshly pulled from the zone depot is polled again, if it still hasn't expired, then there is no choice but to fallback on allocating new memory.

What's all this jazz about deferring and committing? I like to think of a deferred advance as a "fake advance", it snapshots the current sequence but does not increment it, which avoids a global read-modify-write (RMW) operation on the global write sequence. The key idea is that there is no need to advance the sequence, i.e commit it, until we actually need to, and this also serves as an amortization feature because a sequence can be jumped to instantly, for instance, from 1 to 5 instead of individually advancing through 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

The recirculation depot is hence called as such because it allows a given bucket to recirculate and age before given the chance to be reused again.

This SMR scheme, like anything else, has its own tradeoffs. It is relevant to compare it with RCU because both are analogous, compared to RCU:

The best resource, as always, is reading the actual code, which is thankfully very well commented (GUS link, UMA link). The XNU code is also heavily commented (SMR link, zalloc link).

Additionally, these are useful resources:

I have also implemented GUS and an allocator inspired by XNU's and UMA in my own operating system, zag (SMR link, allocator link)

In fact, one could use a timestamp counter such as the TSC for this, as seen in Parallel Sequences. ↩

The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator ↩

Magazines and Vmem: Extending the Slab Allocator to Many CPUs and Arbitrary Resources ↩

I don't know Rust enough to be sure but I don't think so. It only affect the package manager and not the compiler.

There is a risk in Cargo from unused dependencies - Cargo has a build graph based on the declared dependencies in Cargo.toml, and chooses what build steps to run based on that graph. One thing a crate can contain is a build script - which is code that's built and run on the build host at the time of compilation, and can do anything that code running as part of the build system can do.

In theory, an unused dependency can contain a build.rs that's got a security-relevant bug in it; that would then cause a security issue on the build host if you built the unused dependency. Removing it means that's not a problem :-)

Type inference: I prefer explicit/manifest typing for all variables. It also improves code reasoning IMHO. Same problem for code review tools that may lack some features present in the text editor or IDE to show type information when hovering the mouse on a variable name.

The shadowing feature for variables looks to me a bad practice. It should be: one variable name, one usage. So something like

The .. operator versus ..= (creating half-open and closed ranges, respectively). Off-by-one errors are so frequent in programming that such succinct syntax can be misleading when reading quickly some piece of code. Example:

It doesn't follow the more standard mathematics notation:

At some point, in programming languages a more classic for loop with an integer variable is clearer:

Succinct code creates more logic errors IMHO. Even though Rust is much safer with the compiler, I suspect there will be more such kind of logic bugs. Code obfuscation and backdoors are perhaps trickier to detect with such subtle operators.

BTW, the "fn" keyword is not really fun in some countries (political parties).

The lack of a semicolon which means that it's the return value looks also something weird and subtle to catch for the eyes. I prefer an explicit return keyword.

Natural languages have many redundancies (plural forms in a sentence, e.g.). When reading or listening, a small inattention is not a problem because you can catch up thanks to the redundancies.

That was also my opinion when I started programming in Rust. But soon I realized that the return is just redundant and it's actually much easier to read without it. A function always returns something. Even if it's (). Why write `return` then? The last thing is always returned. Rust actually is much more consistent than C and C++ here, where void is kind of a special case. All of the other things you said: You can just do as you wish. Rust doesn't prevent you from adding a return statement to the end of the function. Or adding types to all local variables. Or using full path syntax all over the place, or just use plain C-style function names all over the place, etc. Except for the for-loop thing everything can be done, if you like it better. The for-loop thing can probably easily be implemented with a macro.

Nope. It would be a still-born tech. That's the story with disruptive technologies: they take time AND they are not ready to replace existing technologies — but when they are ready, it's too late to do anything. The story is always the same: it takes X years to develop new technology till it would be ready to replace the old one. With Rust it was 10-20 years (depending from where you start counting), with hydraulic excavators it took 70 years, the whole freaking life… but incumbents only start thinking about doing something disruptive technology is ready — yet they need X more years to finish “the answer to the disruptor”. And by that time… it's too late: technology may even work, but everyone who may want it have already switched, the outliers would use old technology till they would retire, there are literally zero market for you. > It's just that there is currently a lot of social pressure for C developers to start new projects in Rust, or to rewrite progressively existing C codebases to Rust. Precisely. Means it's too late to start with SubC or “subset of superset of C++” (something that was talked for decades, but never materialized). Some people would rewrite C codebases to Rust properly, some would file an LLM and would get some kind of abomination that would look alien to both C and Rust developers… but time have come and we no longer have luxury of talking about other alternatives: they are either ready TODAY or they wouldn't work. Because humans are humans: if it took 10-20 years for Rust to become “good enough” to replace C then it would take the exact same 10-20 years for SubC or “subset of superset of C++” — and people wouldn't wait that long when Rust works here and now.

Fully-qualified function call syntax is possible to use everywhere, again modulo unnameable types, but it looks quite ugly. While I agree that (for example) foo.into() is a bit ambiguous about what conversion we're performing, you can fix that by writing Bar::from(foo) if you prefer. Nobody in their right mind is going to write >::into(foo) or >::from(foo). (Those latter syntaxes exist to disambiguate the case where multiple traits define from() or into() methods or associated functions, or where Foo and Bar have inherent implementations of those methods or associated functions. But From and Into are well-known stdlib traits, so such a collision is unlikely in practice. It would be more plausible with more obscure traits, and fully qualified syntax is commonly used in macros because you can't know ahead of time that a collision is impossible.)

Posted Nov 15, 2026 9:33 UTC (Sun) by adobriyan (guest, #30858) [Link]

shadow_reuse lints cases where you re-use the value, for example maybe "width" on line 10 doesn't including padding but "width" on line 20 onwards adds 10 for padding. shadow_same lints cases where the shadow is just fiddling with the mutability or references, so maybe "goose" on line 10 is an actual Goose, but on line 20 onwards it's now just a mutable reference to the same goose. shadow_unrelated lints almost the opposite case from shadow_reuse, maybe "depth" on line 10 is an integer number of pixels while on line 20 onwards it's a 3D buffer. It might seem as though, since Rust has lints for so many misuses of shadowing, the whole idea of shadowing comes into disrepute, but in fact the argument for shadowing is that it is more readable - when done appropriately. Some codebases where shadowing is forbidden have to work around this. In languages like Rust with a good static type system this can encourage use of weaker, rubbish types and mutability when you'd be better off with immutable strong types and some shadowing. let delay : bool = /* somehow we discover a bool --- yes or no we want a delay here */ let delay : Duration = /* we make a (perhaps zero) Duration -- representing some amount of time */ let delay : MyHTMLType = /* some HTML about that delay */ If you forbid shadowing, you tempt somebody to decide booleans, durations and pointers to some HTML are all just basically integers, so we can say this is an integer and make it mutable then re-assign it, changing what it means repeatedly but sneaking past our "no shadowing" rule. Alternatively maybe they name these variables delay_bool, delay_duration and delay_html but we already HAVE a type system, why are you shovelling this into variable names?

Or, in C: "Lets put this data in this struct field because the field is anyway unused during the code path I'm implementing" kind of hack (instead of adding a new field, or have an union).

See my response elsewhere in the thread (about `combined_hash`) for how Rust users use shadowing as a positive pattern to prevent errors.

The shadowing feature for variables looks to me a bad practice. It should be: one variable name, one usage.

Here's an example from my coding today, to illustrate why shadowing helps prevent errors.

I'm matching a type Foo { hash, .. } => {. I need to combine that hash with another hash, to get the correct hash to use for lookups.

If I used (handwaving) let combined_hash = combine_hashes(hash, other_hash);, then hash is still right there for doing incorrect lookups. I could drop(hash); // to avoid using the wrong one, but that's cumbersome and error-prone; if I don't predict the likely problems and do that.

So I let hash = combine_hashes(hash, other_hash); instead. Now the old hash doesn't exist anymore and you can't mistakenly use it.

Old K&R C used to require some things to be globally unique that no longer need to be, such as field names; this is how we ended up with fields like tv_usec rather than just usec. (Technically, field names could be the same if they had the same type and offset; yikes.) That was an unfortunate limitation. Having to give every local variable a unique name, rather than overwriting it and intentionally making it inaccessible when no longer used, is also an unfortunate limitation.

If your thought on reading the above is "don't have types/methods/etc that complicated": they're not complicated unless you write them out that way, and otherwise this kind of thing arises very naturally.

Consider a HashMap, the kind of type Rust uses very regularly when it's so readily available. Consider the concrete type of the HashMap's iterator over key-value pairs. Consider calling the map method on that iterator, and what concrete type that returns depending on the closure you passed to map. Consider how those would all change if we add a trait Map abstracting over HashMap vs BTreeMap.

Do you actually want to write out all of the methods and types, fully qualified? Including for every intermediate value you might have?

Posted Nov 18, 2026 10:44 UTC (Wed) by swilmet (guest, #98424) [Link] (1 responses)

I got annoyed that Rust wouldn't let me do some things that I could have done in C.

BTW, Rust is really good at forcing a good internal architecture, having a tree of values instead of a sea of objects. I sometimes say A DAG of components instead of a spaghetti architecture.

E.g., in a protocol that allows different nodes to publish and re-publish data-objects (a common pattern in networking); - given a neighbour, you must be able to retrieve the subset of data-objects which were received from it (e.g., so you can clean up data-objects if a neighbour goes away, etc.) - given a data-object, you must be able to retrieve the subset of neighbours you received the data-object from - independently of any neighbours, you must be able to retrieve the set of all data-objects (data-objects can have lifetimes independent of neighbours) One approach is to directly cross-link the data structures that represent neighbours and data-objects, so you can always do the necessary walk (even if inefficient), as long as you maintain at least one general index of all neighbours, and/or of all data-objects. However, you can not do this in safe Rust. Another approach is to maintain multiple indexes. E.g., a set data-structure for all neighbours, a set data-structure for all data-objects, a map of lists for neighbour->list of data-objects, a map of lists for data-object -> list of neighbours. AFAIK, you can't do this in safe Rust either - even assuming you have safe sets, lists, maps [and allowing those to use unsafe internally] from your library. You can't share mutable references between indices, so you either need to unsafely store mutable references (but then why Rust?) or do a temporary remove-modify-reinsert for all indices plus an unsafe cast to mutable to modify either a neighbour or data-object. Or you do what (AFAICT) nearly all long-lived, safe, Rust code does that has to manage non-trivial relations between objects that are simply intrinsic to /many/ problem domains: use reference-counting (but.... then why Rust?).

- given a neighbour, you must be able to retrieve the subset of data-objects which were received from it (e.g., so you can clean up data-objects if a neighbour goes away, etc.) - given a data-object, you must be able to retrieve the subset of neighbours you received the data-object from - independently of any neighbours, you must be able to retrieve the set of all data-objects (data-objects can have lifetimes independent of neighbours) One approach is to directly cross-link the data structures that represent neighbours and data-objects, so you can always do the necessary walk (even if inefficient), as long as you maintain at least one general index of all neighbours, and/or of all data-objects. AFAIK, you can't do this in safe Rust either - even assuming you have safe sets, lists, maps [and allowing those to use unsafe internally] from your library. You can't share mutable references between indices, so you either need to unsafely store mutable references (but then why Rust?) or do a temporary remove-modify-reinsert for all indices plus an unsafe cast to mutable to modify either a neighbour or data-object. Or you do what (AFAICT) nearly all long-lived, safe, Rust code does that has to manage non-trivial relations between objects that are simply intrinsic to /many/ problem domains: use reference-counting (but.... then why Rust?).

One approach is to directly cross-link the data structures that represent neighbours and data-objects, so you can always do the necessary walk (even if inefficient), as long as you maintain at least one general index of all neighbours, and/or of all data-objects. However, you can not do this in safe Rust. Another approach is to maintain multiple indexes. E.g., a set data-structure for all neighbours, a set data-structure for all data-objects, a map of lists for neighbour->list of data-objects, a map of lists for data-object -> list of neighbours. I disagree that ranges are less readable than manual indexing, though. But I agree that the range syntax could have been better if we had perfect foresight.

InfoQ Homepage News How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development Without Overloading Developers' Machines

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read

To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.

In fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".

Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:

With Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.

Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.

Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can

implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the issue, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.

The platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.

Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.

Commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.

Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9794. SecurityDataPipeline.com Launches as a New Educational Resource for the AI Era

The ungated resource explains how security data pipelines reduce SIEM ingestion costs, preserve detection coverage, and prepare the data layer for AI-driven security operations.

BOSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Realm Security today launched SecurityDataPipeline.com, a new educational resource designed to help cybersecurity professionals understand security data pipelines and reduce SIEM costs without weakening detection coverage.

For many security teams, rising data volumes present a difficult choice between cutting data and keeping detections. Security data pipelines offer a way to address this challenge. Because they sit between security data sources and destinations, these platforms collect, process, filter, and route telemetry before it reaches a SIEM, data lake, or other security tool.

"Most security teams are being asked to cut SIEM spend and roll out AI agents at the same time, and both of those decisions come down to the data layer," said Chris O'Brien, VP of Marketing at Realm Security. "We built SecurityDataPipeline.com so practitioners can understand how pipelines work and how to reduce volume without losing detections, before they ever talk to a vendor, including us."

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Security data pipelines are becoming essential infrastructure as AI reshapes the SOC. As enterprises deploy AI agents for triage, investigation, and response, the data layer underneath those agents determines whether those agents get clean, normalized context to reason over. SecurityDataPipeline.com is a resource for security leaders trying to understand how to turn raw logs and fragmented cybersecurity data into clean, actionable intelligence for AI SOC agents and other AI cybersecurity initiatives.

The resource also covers how security data pipelines route telemetry to destinations including Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, and Databricks Delta Lake; how OCSF-normalized data supports AI SOC agents; and how MITRE ATT&CK coverage can be preserved as teams reduce SIEM ingestion volumes.

On SecurityDataPipeline.com, visitors can:

Explore a beginner's guide explaining security data pipelines and their core functions.

Try an ungated interactive pipeline demonstration showing how security events are filtered, transformed, enriched, and routed.

Use a SIEM cost calculator estimating potential reductions in data ingestion costs.

Learn about practical use cases covering SIEM cost reduction, SIEM migration, SOC efficiency, data governance, and AI readiness.

Read technology comparisons explaining the differences between security data pipelines, SIEMs, data lakes, log forwarders, and observability pipelines.

The resource addresses how to reduce the cost of managing security data without weakening detection capabilities by looking at the role of data filtering, normalization, enrichment, routing, and retention. It also shows how teams can identify which information their security detections need and which data can be stored more economically.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

The website is intended for CISOs, security architects, SOC managers, and cybersecurity professionals evaluating ways to manage growing telemetry volumes.

SecurityDataPipeline.com is available at https://securitydatapipeline.com/.

Realm Security gives security teams independent control over their telemetry before it reaches the SIEM, data lake, or AI agent. The platform understands what each source produces and what each downstream system needs, then guides teams on what to keep, archive, and route. Headquartered in Boston, Realm deploys in about a week and typically cuts SIEM ingestion costs by 50% or more. Learn more at www.realm.security.

#9793. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#9791. APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

After compromising websites, the Russian state-sponsored threat group is fingerprinting victims, then harvesting information from the interesting ones.

It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.

The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.

Researchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible.

"Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation."

Related:ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI

APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions.

Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.

In its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel.

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.

The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Each chain targeted specific vulnerabilities in iOS or Android that had remained unpatched on the exposed devices.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

Sekoia said it found several indicators linking the campaign to APT29, including remnants of a separate 2025 watering-hole operation that researchers have previously attributed to the group. Sekoia also found signs that the attackers may have obtained their exploits from a third party, possibly a commercial surveillance vendor (CSV). The campaign's victims include organizations in Europe and the US, though most are based in Ukraine, a country that Russian threat groups have incessantly targeted since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

APT29's latest campaign is another indication of how mobile devices have become attractive intelligence targets for threat groups. Commercial spyware vendors are fueling the trend by making technology available that enables large scale surveillance and data theft via mobile devices. APT29's likely sourcing of the DarkSword exploit kit from a third-party provider suggests that sophisticated mobile intrusion capabilities that were once largely associated with highly targeted espionage operations are finding their way into broader campaigns.

"The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation," Sekoia warned. "Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9789. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9788. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

#9787. Announcing XRAID: declustered parity RAID for zoned XFS

Christoph Hellwig has announced the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS.

The two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...]

Work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it.

The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a new "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems. We have also extended Zonar (The zoned file-system visualisation tool) to show how each logical zone maps onto physical zones on devices.

Hellwig gave a presentation at FOSSY in August on this topic; video of the talk does not seem to be available yet, but his slides are available.

Yeah, ZFS has dRAID, but that doesn't mean new systems have to replicate its filesystem coupling.

I'm not saying that an interface that supports these use cases well and is generic enough to allow stacking cannot be made, but we simply do not have one.

Remember the days when we used to build systems out of pluggable components talking to each other over generic interfaces? […] Couldn't it therefore behave like a zoned block device via DM instead of having to be integrated into a specific filesystem?

Now I cannot talk about XRAID; I haven’t looked into it, and maybe it’d easily work the way you envision it.

But as a general answer: because ZFS, but also others like APFS etc, have realized that block layer abstractions are comparatively crude and often operate at the wrong level. Most filesystem subsystems do not care about blocks, but actually operate on a semantic "file-level" themselves.

For example, as a filesystem I don’t want to encrypt opaque blocks, but files. I don’t want to checksum opaque 4K hardware blocks, I want to checksum files. I don’t want to snapshot storage blocks, I want to snapshot files.

Once you’re able to detach those concepts from real or virtual blocks, you immediately gain much more freedom. With encryption for example you can now suddenly start complex hierarchies without the need to separate things into block-layer partitions. With checksumming, you can now configure your algorithm and chunk size depending on your needs and capabilities (which is still highly relevant for dedup).

And this is not also resolvable: At some point all those features would require insights about the filesystem’s inner workings and structure. So you either stop at this point and keep things separated but imperfect; or you start to define more and more information channels between the filesystem and the block-layer, until you effectively give up on that layer separation anyways – in the end you’ll get an inseparable mess of components that were not really designed with each other in mind and now are imperfectly tied together nonetheless.

And then we also have the advantage of development being self-contained: You are independent of other systems and their development cycle – once your component actually gets used by other filesystems, development immediately becomes more and more ossified; maybe even up to a point where any further meaningful development would require changes that are fundamentally incompatible with other consumers.

As I said, with XRAID I don’t know, but tl;dr: In general "modern" filesystem development has shifted away from block-layer abstractions. I don’t know any real-world 4th-gen filesystem that actively builds its first-class features on top of block-layer composition, and AFAIK even the in-house "contenders" like Btrfs or Bcachefs don’t use them much. That is for a reason.

https://youtu.be/79fvDDPaIoY?si=JkCTFX6J6T-s19rE&t=345

It's not part of AVX512 - it's part of the GFNI ISA extension, and on page 3-470 of Vol. 2A of the Intel SDM from December 2021, it's described as needing AVX and GFNI if operating unmasked on XMM or YMM registers, AVX512F if operating on ZMM registers, and AVX512VL if operating masked on XMM or YMM registers.

There's also a gf2p8mulb instruction, which is part of the basic GFNI set, and operates on XMM registers; this is a 2 operand form (where vgf2p8mulb is a 3 operand form), using the first register as both first source operand and a result destination. The VEX (AVX) and EVEX (AVX512) encoded forms have a separate register for destination and the first source operand, and the EVEX encoded form is the only one that supports a write mask.

In which case, it needs GFNI and AVX512F.

I'm not aware of any server CPUs (Xeon or EPYC) that have GFNI but not AVX512, which might explain your confusion.

AMD either supports both, or neither. Intel supports both on Xeons, but has Core, Celeron, Pentium and Atom variants that only have GFNI; indeed, some Tremont-based Intel Atom CPUs have GFNI but not even AVX2, only supporting gf2p8mulb and not vgf2p8mulb.

#9786. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.
