#9729. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9726. Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Forks of the open source Artex framework, along with 45 similar pen-testing tools, remain capable of executing credential attacks and cloud breaches at machine speed across multiple industries.

AI penetration-testing tool Artex has proven to be a boon for threat actors large and small, taking familiar attacker playbooks and deploying them at machine speeds — ushering in a potentially new era for defenders looking to get ahead of AI-enabled threats.

In July, independent developer Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. It is, by intention, a legitimate tool. However, as is so often the case with pen-test tools (such as, famously, Cobalt Strike), threat actors found a way to take advantage of it for malicious use. By late summer and early fall, a range of threat actors were using it as part of their toolkit.

Artex is capable of brute-forcing passwords, dumping databases, enumerating and abusing APIs, and more. This positions it for credential compromise and lateral movement in its own right, but the agentic element means Artex can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft saw an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes, for example.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, tells Dark Reading that while legitimate tool misuse is a known quantity, AI reduces the effort and expertise required to execute complex attacks. "What is particularly noteworthy about the Artex campaigns is the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy," he says. "Activities that previously required deliberate integration can now be chained together and executed with limited hacking skills."

At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository due to rampant abuse, but many forks of the tool remain, so the threat remains. But even if all the forks went offline and Artex was no longer a going concern, the underlying threat of frameworks like it is far from over.

GitGuardian yesterday, for instance, detailed 45 different agentic attack frameworks (Artex "siblings" as the researchers called them) that are all capable of conducting attacks autonomously with the help of an AI model. Depending on the tool, these pen-testing frameworks are capable of end-to-end attacks against a network, Web application targeting, and/or autonomous coding. Some even include built-in command-and-control functionality. That's not to say these tools are inherently bad — pen-testing tools have many legitimate use cases — but it does illustrate the wide range of options for today's attacker.

The best-known incident to date involved China's Storm-0940, which adapted Artex source code into its own offensive infrastructure. Last month, around Oct. 10, the actor used the Artex framework to launch a massive password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 specific user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests in the process. On average, this represented 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alert.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

When this largely failed, Storm-0940 pivoted to target ConnectWise's internal infrastructure. Attackers exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials belonging to ConnectWise's Cloud Backup application, allowing them to compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Abuse extends far beyond a single threat actor or objective. Microsoft last week published a blog post discussing how a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster tracked as Storm-3358 started using Artex in its attacks against financial organizations primarily (but not exclusively) in Southeast Asia. Microsoft said it observed Storm-3358 using Artex in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public Internet, exploit vulnerabilities, and install open source remote access Trojans (RATs).

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

Microsoft added that other threat actors have used Artex agents "to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in Web applications, use Web shells for persistence on compromised Web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration."

CrowdStrike on Oct. 29 connected Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, India's CERT (CERT-In) tracked a financially motivated threat actor hitting financial institutions, and as of Nov. 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments. That said, because Internet exposure is not required for use, Censys estimated actual global use to be higher.

Recent Artex activity stands out because much of the story involves things security practitioners have seen time and time again. Pen-test tool abuse, nation-state tooling moving downstream to financially motivated attackers, password spraying, supply chain attacks, AI — it's a threat intelligence greatest hits album. But Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, tells Dark Reading what stands out to him most is the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to accomplish the user's goals.

"At GitGuardian, we wanted to see how Artex handles secrets, so we ran it in a sealed lab," he says. "Artex ships no secret scanner, yet in every run where it acted, it found eight of the nine secrets. This included an AWS key recovered from git history. The model improvises on its hunt to reach the Artex user's goals."

Matt Snyder, Aviatrix head of security operations and threat research, says he was most surprised at how, despite the sophisticated nature of Artex's framework, the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying it appears to be low (given how many hosts remain Internet-exposed).

"AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. The framework may be sophisticated, but the operational security surrounding many deployments is not," Snyder says. "This creates a dangerous combination in which more people can launch capable attacks, while poor security leaves their infrastructure, tooling, and potentially victim information exposed to anyone on the Internet."

Increasing sophistication for lower-grade attackers means, as always, defenders should be ready. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering tools like defensive honeypots, which trick attackers into thinking they netted a valuable target.

Check Point advised in a blog post last week that organizations should expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure. "Internet-facing systems should be continuously tested and hardened, with particular attention paid to weak authentication, exposed APIs, credential leakage, remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities and cloud storage permissions," the blog post read.

Censys principal security researcher Silas Cutler offered encouraging words. Because the underlying tradecraft is conventional, the fundamentals still hold, he said, "Enforce MFA, monitor your attack surface, and practice good credential hygiene."

#9724. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

While the cornucopia of CVEs this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he says via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

#9721. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support

#9720. N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

The RMM provider also released a hotfix as a recommended mitigation to address public exploits for the alleged zero-days, which allow for attacker takeover.

N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers who broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers are already scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least the beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

#9717. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9716. AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

An organization's ability to quickly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

"AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your new competitive advantage."

Two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating new dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more important than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil said.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover quickly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:NIST Finalizes Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance, GAO Offers a Reality Check

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he said.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he said. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover quickly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project."

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally important. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

The key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell says. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

In enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read

LinkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.

Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post)

LinkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the company moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.

LinkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.

With Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.

Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post)

Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,

Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.

The deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.

LinkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The company also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.

The converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

#9713. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9712. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9709. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

 


Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

1) What is an NFT?

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

2) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

3) What makes an NFT valuable?


The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

4) How do NFTs work?

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. 

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. 

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

10) How do we buy an NFTs?

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

11) Can i mint NFT for free?

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it?

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

12) Why are people investing so much in NFT?


 Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

Final Saying

That’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below. Also I have a question for you, Is bitcoin an NFTs? let me know in The comment section below

#9708. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9707. AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

この対策パッケージには、官民合同のサイバー対応チーム、経済省が主導するAI専門チーム、および政府の新たな能動的サイバー防衛権限の行使に関する裁量の拡大が含まれている。

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

日本においてサイバー攻撃や情報漏洩が急増していることを受け、日本政府は、攻撃に迅速に対応し、インフラのセキュリティを強化するための産官の専門家チームを設立することを目的とした、100億円（6,300万ドル）規模の緊急サイバーセキュリティ対策パッケージを可決した。

この戦略の4つの柱には、サイバー防衛へのAI導入を含む基礎的なサイバーセキュリティ対策の全国的な徹底、国内のサイバー捜査能力の強化、サイバー攻撃の被害者への支援拡充、そして民間企業と連携してサイバー攻撃に共同で対応することが含まれている。

高市早苗首相は、国のサイバーレジリエンス（回復力）を高めるため、これらのサイバーセキュリティ対策を「迅速かつ効果的に」実施するよう求めた。

「今この瞬間も、不正アクセスや情報漏洩の事案が後を絶たず、人々の日常生活や企業活動に多大な影響を及ぼしている」と、高市早苗首相は11月6日に緊急対策パッケージを発表した際の声明で述べた。「政府のあらゆる資源を動員し、サイバー攻撃への対応能力を全面的に強化していこう。」

サイバー攻撃の急増は、日本企業や政府機関に甚大な被害をもたらしている。サイバーセキュリティ企業（旧トレンドマイクロ）であるTrendAIのデータによると、2026年の最初の9か月間で600件以上のサイバーセキュリティインシデントが公表され、2025年通年の594件を上回った。公表されている報告数は控えめな推計に過ぎない。日本の個人情報保護監督機関は、4月から10月中旬にかけて2,094件の情報漏洩事案を記録しており（原文は日本語）、これも2025年度通年の総件数を上回っている。

他の地域ではAIが攻撃者を支援しているものの、サイバーセキュリティ企業TrendAIの脅威調査共同責任者であるライアン・フローレス氏は、脅威に関する声明の中で、インシデントの増加と攻撃者によるAIの利用との間に明確な関連性は確認されていないと述べた。

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

「サイバー攻撃は世界的に増加しており、その結果として侵害やデータ漏洩も増加しています」と同氏は述べた。「AIが直接関与しているわけではないかもしれませんが、攻撃者が標的を見つけたり、操作を自動化したりするのを支援するAIの能力により、サイバー攻撃は大規模化しています。組織は、被害に遭う確率を下げるために、サイバーリスクを低減し、脆弱性を解消する必要があります。」

最近の侵害事例には、冷凍食品大手のニチレイやビール・食品大手のアサヒに対するランサムウェア攻撃、およびGMOインターネットグループを標的としたデータ侵害などが含まれる。これらの攻撃の多くは犯罪的な性質を持つが、盗まれた情報が他の犯罪グループや国家主体のアクターによって、日本の国民に対して悪用される可能性があることが懸念されていると、日本の通信大手NTTのチーフ・サイバーセキュリティ・ストラテジスト、松原美穂子氏は指摘する。

「攻撃者が十分な個人情報を収集・集約できれば、個人の嗜好から経済活動に至るまで、日本国民の詳細なプロファイルを構築できる」と同氏は述べる。「そのデータは、世論を操作したり、日本の機関に対する信頼を損なわせたりするための標的型偽情報キャンペーンなど、日本に対する影響工作に利用される可能性がある」

日本政府は、緊急資金を活用して、サイバーセキュリティ体制全体を強化するための4つの広範な取り組みを推進する意向だ。閣僚会議の公表された議事録によると、政府は、最近の多くの情報漏洩は適切なセキュリティ対策によって防ぐことができたはずだと指摘し、最初の取り組みとして、各組織が基本的なサイバーセキュリティ対策を確実に実施するよう促すとしている。

2つ目の主要な取り組みは、調査および情報収集能力を向上させ、より精度の高い分析を可能にし、その結果を国民に提供することで、攻撃への備えを強化することである。第三に、政府はサイバー攻撃への対応を強化し、国際的なパートナーシップを構築するとともに、積極的なサイバー防衛措置を実施する。最後に、政府は被害者を支援する能力とインフラを整備し、市民が損害を回復し、企業が事業を継続できるようにする計画だ。

「被害を受けた組織や個人が迷うことなく支援を受けられるよう、利用しやすい相談窓口や専門家による直接的な支援を拡充し、二次被害を防ぐための情報共有を強化する」と、日本の議事録には記されている。「また、官民の専門家を柔軟に派遣するための全国的な仕組みの構築にも着手する」

10月1日、日本の「積極的サイバー防衛法」が施行され、警察や自衛隊（SDF）に対し、日本の国家安全保障にリスクをもたらすあらゆるサイバー攻撃に対して強力な措置を講じる権限が与えられた。

「多くの国が、日本がいかなる種類のサイバー攻撃に対して、どれほどの速さで、どの程度の強度で対応できるのかを知りたがっているだろう」とNTTの松原氏は述べ、次のように付け加えた。「この緊急対策パッケージは……法律の枠組みを経済全体にわたる実用的な能力へと転換し、攻撃の可能性が高まる中、あらゆる規模の組織が攻撃を予防、検知、対応できるよう準備するために必要である。」

しかし、この資金はあくまで第一歩に過ぎず、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの投資を継続するには、さらなる資金が必要になると同氏は指摘する。

「この対策パッケージの重要な点は、サイバーセキュリティを個々の組織に完全に任せておくことはできないという認識が示されていることだ」と松原氏は述べる。「セキュリティ評価やインシデント対応、復旧支援といった形の政府による支援が、大きな違いを生むことができる。」
