#9668. A Beginner's Guide to Classes and Objects in C++

C++ remains a foundational language in the programming landscape, recognized for its adaptability and high performance. It’s useful to understand its core principles, not only for efficient programming but also because many companies rely on it for their critical applications. This article provides an overview of the fundamental concepts that every newcomer to C++ should be familiar with.

Object-Oriented Programming is a paradigm centered around objects and classes. It’s not just a feature of C++ but a fundamental aspect that shapes how we approach problem-solving in software development. OOP offers several benefits:

A class in C++ is akin to a blueprint for creating objects. It encapsulates data and methods for interaction. A class defines the attributes (member variables) and behaviors (member functions or methods) of its objects.

A class is declared with the keyword class followed by the class name.

Inside the class, members can be categorized by access specifiers:

Member Variables: These are the attributes of the class, representing the data.

Member Functions: These functions operate on the member variables, defining the behavior of the class.

In this article we are going to take a look only on public and private members.

Whats important to say, we are going to define classes in .h file or .hpp file, all of the functions which are defined in the class, will be defined in .cpp file, its a good practise in c++, to separate them.

By itself, this class doesn’t do much. To give functionality, we need to add parameters inside the class.

In our Car class example, you may notice the use of private member variables (_brand, _model, and _year) and may wonder why they are not declared as public. The answer lies in one of the core principles of Object-Oriented Programming: encapsulation.

Encapsulation is the mechanism of restricting direct access to some of an object’s components, which can prevent the accidental modification of data. It also reduces system complexity and increases robustness by allowing the developer to restrict what is accessible to the outside world.

The public members of a class, like the constructor, destructor, displayCar(), and updateYear(int newYear), form the class's interface with the outside world. These are what users of the class see and interact with.

Lets talk a bit more about Constructor, which has an extremly important role in C++.

Initialization: Constructors ensure that objects start their life in a consistent state. For example, when you create a Car object, the constructor initializes the car's brand, model, and year. This guarantees that every Car object is properly set up before it's used.

Control: Constructors provide control over how and with what parameters objects are created. You can define multiple constructors with different parameters, allowing for different initialization scenarios.

Resource Allocation: In more complex classes, constructors can also handle resource allocation, like dynamically allocating memory. This ensures that the object has everything it needs to function properly right from the start.

In our Car class example, the constructor is defined as follows:

This constructor takes three parameters: xBrand, xModel, and xYear, which are used to initialize the _brand, _model, and _year private member variables of the class. When a new Car object is created, this constructor is automatically invoked:

Here, myCar is an instance of the Car class, and it is being created with the brand "Toyota", model "Corolla", and year 2020. This instantiation calls the constructor, setting up myCar with these specific values.

In our example we will define the class structure in a .h or .hpp file and implement its functions, including the constructor, in a .cpp file. This separation enhances readability and maintainability.

In C++, when we define the member functions of a class outside of the class declaration (usually in a .cpp file), we use the scope resolution operator ::. This operator specifies that the following function is a member of a particular class. Let's break this down with respect to our Car class example:

Car:: is the scope resolution operator. It is used to define the member functions of the Car class outside the class declaration.

It tells the compiler that the function being defined belongs to the Car class.

Here, Car::Car signifies that this constructor function is a member of the Car class.

For other member functions like displayCar and updateYear:

The Car:: before displayCar() and updateYear() indicates that these functions are members of the Car class.

Clarity: It provides clarity, especially when the same function name is used in different classes.

Organization: It helps in keeping the class declaration (in .h or .hpp files) separate from the implementation (in .cpp files), which is a good practice for larger projects.

Linkage: It ensures that the correct function associated with the appropriate class is called, particularly important in cases of inheritance and polymorphism.

When you see a line like Car::displayCar(), it means that the function displayCar() is being defined for the Car class. It's not just any function named displayCar but specifically the one that belongs to Car.

This method of organization is standard in C++ and is critical for maintaining code in larger projects where multiple classes may have functions with the same name. It avoids confusion and ensures that the correct function is linked during compilation. So, what is left for us, lets build a main for our class to see how it works.

In our example, we create a Car object using the line:

The Car constructor is called with the arguments “Toyota”, “Corolla”, and 2015. This sets up the myCar object with these initial values.

The state of an object is represented by its attributes (member variables).

These attributes are private to the Car class and are initialized via the constructor.

The behavior of an object is defined by its methods (member functions).

After creation, we interact with myCar using its methods.

Calling myCar.displayCar() prints the current state of myCar.

myCar.updateYear(2020) changes the year attribute of myCar to 2020.

Another call to myCar.displayCar() shows the updated state.

The lifetime of myCar is the duration of the main() function.

It is created when the main() function executes and destroyed when main() ends.

The destructor ~Car() is called automatically at the end of main(), signifying the end of the myCar object's lifetime.

Objects are the cornerstone of OOP. They allow programmers to create modular, reusable, and scalable code. Each object operates independently, with its internal state and behaviors, making code more organized and easier to manage.

As we wrap up this beginner’s guide to C++, we’ve explored the fundamental concepts of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) and how they are implemented in the C++ language. From understanding what classes are to diving into the specifics of constructors, destructors, and access specifiers, we’ve covered the essentials that lay the groundwork for effective C++ programming.

Remember, the power of C++ lies in its ability to encapsulate data and functionalities within classes, promoting modularity, reusability, and robustness in software development. The Car class example we discussed is just a glimpse into the vast potential of C++. By keeping member variables private and exposing public methods, we ensure that our objects maintain their integrity and are used as intended.

As you continue to explore C++, you’ll encounter more complex concepts such as inheritance, polymorphism, templates, and the Standard Template Library (STL). Each of these concepts builds on the foundations laid by understanding classes and objects.

Happy coding, and welcome to the world of C++ programming!

#9667. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

#9666. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9665. Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Large language models and other AI systems allow a growing number of ransomware groups to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data quickly.

Ransomware attacks are expanding amid cybercriminals' increasing use of AI tools, but at the same time, fewer organizations are paying ransoms, according to multiple reports released this month.

Globally, organizations are seeing far more ransomware incidents, while the number of attacks targeting US companies has remained fairly steady. In the third quarter of 2026, for example, ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches, an increase of nearly 40% over the previous quarter, according to threat data released by cybersecurity services firm Halcyon.

Threat groups adopting AI is likely a major reason for the increase in attacks. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to create convincing social-engineering messaging, find sensitive data quickly, and assist attackers has largely driven the surge in attacks in other nations, says Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and a former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Cyber Division.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"We think AI is a big part of [the growth] because it has removed the language barrier for phishing," she says. "We're now seeing much more convincing phishing in Japanese, for example. Countries like Japan are treating this almost as a state of emergency."

Overall, the jump in claimed ransomware cases — up 31% from the first quarter and 39% from the second, according to Halcyon's report — has not necessarily resulted in more ransoms paid out.

Take the retail sector as an example: While 62% of attacks on companies succeeded in encrypting data — up from 48% in 2025 — less than a third (32%) of retailers actually paid to get the data back, nearly half of the 58% that paid in 2025, according to Sophos's "The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026" report.

Instead, a solid majority of retail firms (71%) recovered their data from backup, and most recovered within a week, Sophos found. Other sectors, such as local government and school districts, have seen declines in paying ransomware as well, says Chester Wisniewski, global field chief information security officer (CISO) at Sophos.

"None of them are paying the ransom," he says. "Whether there's extortion involved, whether data theft's involved, it kind of doesn't matter. They're largely not paying the ransom."

The number of ransomware groups claiming success took off in 2026, growing from 75 in the first quarter to 111 in the third, according to Halcyon data. While ransom amounts have continued to decline, the growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat to companies, Sophos's Wisniewski says.

Related:Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

"There's been five or six new names I've seen in just the last few weeks, so it doesn't seem like ransomware's going away at all," he says. "But its efficacy has been declining as far as generating actual money for the crooks."

The median ransom demand has dropped to $700,000 in 2026, from $2 million in 2024, according to Sophos data.

That hasn't stopped new ransomware groups from continuing to appear. At the end of the quarter, about a third of all claimed ransomware successes came from groups that didn’t exist six months earlier, says Duy-Phuc Pham, a malware researcher at Trellix.

"At the top, The Gentlemen grew from a few dozen victims a year ago to the most active group, ahead of Qilin," he says. "That kind of success makes them the obvious next target for law enforcement, which spent this year going after the shared services these groups depend on, from criminal VPNs to laundering services."

With attackers increasingly using AI, ransomware gangs will continue to broaden their campaigns against more industries in more regions — part of the reason that Europe has witnessed an increase in attacks, while US victims' share of incidents has remained the same or decreased, says Pham. AI allows attackers to create more convincing social-engineering messaging in a variety of languages, removing a significant historical barrier to targeting smaller populations.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

Because of the greater scale that AI enables attackers to hit, ransomware threat actors are able to widen their coverage, he says.

"When a tool can scan, exploit, and move through networks with little human effort, a small crew can do the work of a large one, hit far more victims, and do it faster," Pham says. "That fits what we see on the leak sites: more groups and more newcomers."

The manufacturing sector continues to be the top target of ransomware gangs, because suppliers and partners often share the same platforms, so a single compromise can expose engineering data beyond the targeted company, says Halcyon's Kaiser.

The sector will likely continue to be the top targeted group in 2027, especially as international organizations continue to account for a greater share in the coming year, she says.

"I'd expect continued growth, especially outside the US," Kaiser says. "The big open question is whether more attacks means more money ... countries newly feeling the pain are paying much more attention, which should improve international cooperation."

#9664. How to Manage Game Art Projects Without Being an Artist

Game project manager (~10 years). Author of PMNote — https://pmnote.ai

Game project manager (~10 years). Author of PMNote — https://pmnote.ai

Game project manager (~10 years). Author of PMNote — https://pmnote.ai

A Monday scheduling meeting. Art reports the estimate: this character still needs five days. You cannot tell what those five days cover — five more days of concept art, or modeling and animation as well? You are not an artist, so you do not press, and you nod. Two weeks later the character is still not in the build. When you ask, the answer is that concept art was revised once in the middle.

Many PMs get stuck here. I am Hao, in my 10th year as a game PM, originally a game designer, and I now write Hao’s Game PM Notes (Hao的游戏PM笔记). I was a PM who did not understand art and was then pushed to manage the art line. This piece is how I think game art project management should be done, written for people in the same position.

One reassuring point first: you do not need to know how to draw in order to manage art. You need to treat art as a production process.

To a PM, art often looks like a black box. Once you take it apart, it becomes clear.

Game art assets fall roughly into two kinds: the character line and the scene line. The character line starts from concept and design, then goes through 3D modeling, texturing, and skeletal animation, and finally enters the engine. The scene line has similar stages, but more parallelism: several scenes can go to different people at the same time. The scheduling logic differs. The character line is mostly serial — the next stage cannot start until the previous one is done. The scene line can add people to buy time. UI and VFX have a process structure similar to the character line, so the same breakdown applies; I will not discuss them separately below.

The first thing I did when I took over the art line was to schedule these two lines separately. Mixed together, the character work got stuck, the scene people waited, and every weekly meeting was spent explaining another slip.

One more principle is a lifesaver: stage output should be something that can actually run, not a work-in-progress file. A signed-off concept piece does not count as output. A character that can be turned around in the engine does. Process files can mislead you. Something that runs will not.

For a PM without an art background, asking for an estimate is the scariest part. Ask “how many days are left,” and the answer is always “two more days.” Those two days can last two weeks.

Break the asset into steps and ask about those. Do not ask whether a character is “done.” Ask whether concept has been approved, what stage modeling is in, who is doing the textures, and whether animation has been scheduled. Each step has a rough reference duration. Whichever step has overrun is where the problem is hiding. You do not need to do the work. You only need to ask questions against a step list.

Progress reports should change with this. Do not ask “is it finished?” Ask “which step is it in now, how many days has this step already taken, and who picks it up next?” After those three questions, real progress surfaces on its own. “This character still needs five days” becomes: how many days has concept already taken, and when will it be handed to modeling. Once the number is attached to a step, it is much harder to stay vague.

Art outsourcing is where schedule and quality risk concentrate most heavily. The failure pattern I have seen most often is this: the request is briefed verbally, nobody looks at the work in the middle, the file is opened the night before delivery, the style and the specs are wrong, it goes back for rework, and the version milestone is blown through.

The responsibility usually does not sit with the vendor. It sits in the handoff. There are four management actions:

Put the handoff on paper. Write the request, reference images, spec parameters, and naming rules into a handoff sheet, and start only after both sides have confirmed it. Saying “I want that kind of feel” out loud is an invitation to improvise.

Put the mid-point check at one-third, not at the end. If you wait until the work is finished before you look, it is already too late. A review at one-third is when a wrong direction is cheapest to correct.

Give the acceptance criteria in advance. The vendor should know, before work starts, what acceptance will look at. Adding requirements at the last minute is a main source of disputes.

Leave a channel for escalating problems. The most expensive case is a vendor that gets stuck, says nothing, and toughs it out until the last day. Say this clearly at the start: if you are blocked, report it at any time; an early report will not be treated as a fault.

Half of the work of managing art sits at the boundaries.

Design speaks in “feel”: more ornate, more oppressive. Engineering speaks in “specs”: the polycount is over the limit, the bone count has to be cut. Art speaks in “look”: this light bake has to be done again.

The three sides are not speaking the same language. The PM translates “feel” into reference images and priorities, “specs” into change items that art can execute, and “look” into schedule numbers that can be put on the table in a meeting.

Requirement changes also explode at this boundary. Design revises a request, and three days of art work disappear. Changes need a record and a visible cost: which steps this change affects, and how many days it adds, should be put in the open. People become more careful once that is visible.

Art risk does not need daily watching. Three signals a week are enough.

Stuck tasks. If the same step has sat past its reference duration, go and ask.

Change frequency. If one asset line is changed more than twice in a week, the upstream request has not been thought through. Block the source; do not only clean up downstream.

Outsourcing rework rate. If the same vendor is sent back for rework repeatedly, first check whether the handoff sheet exists only on paper, and only then consider changing vendors.

Behind these three signals is a simple tracking sheet. Half an hour a week going through it is far better than discovering a general delay at the end of the month.

The entry path is plain: take the black box apart into a process, replace “feel” with steps, and replace verbal agreements with paper. The rest is practice.

Yes. A PM manages process, schedule, quality, and collaboration, none of which require an art foundation. What you need to add is two things: the production process for art assets, and the basic terms. Leave aesthetic judgment to the art lead. Use your judgment on whether the process is reasonable.

Break it open by step. If every step is within its reference range and the total has still overrun, it is a scheduling problem: adjust the plan or add people. If one step is clearly overtime, look at the specific blockage: repeated revision, unfamiliar tools, or an unclear request. “Cannot be finished” carries no information by itself. It only does once you take it apart.

First check your own handoff sheet and acceptance criteria. If those two are unclear, the result will wobble no matter which vendor you switch to. If it is still unstable after the handoff is clear, look at fit. Some teams are strong at characters, some at scenes; assigning the wrong kind of work can also look like “unstable quality.”

The art lead is responsible for art quality and style. The art PM is responsible for the schedule, the process, cross-functional collaboration, and outsourcing. In short, the lead watches whether it looks good; the PM watches whether it is on time and running smoothly. On projects where the two work well together, the art line rarely runs into serious trouble.

The public Chinese original is here: How to manage game art when you are not an artist.

#9663. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9662. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

Pros

  • It takes only a few minutes to set up an online store and begin selling products.
  • You can sell your products on a single storefront, even if you are selling multiple product types.
  • Sellfy supports selling a variety of product types, including physical items, digital goods, subscriptions, and print-on-demand products.

  • Sellfy offers a free plan for those who want to test out the features before committing to a paid plan.
  • You get paid the same day you make a sale. Sellfy doesn't delay your funds as some other payment processors do. 
  • Print-on-demand services are available directly from your store, so you can sell merchandise to fans without setting up an integration. 
  • You can conduct all store-related activities via the mobile app and all online stores have mobile responsive designs.
  • Everything you need to make your website is included, including a custom domain name hosting, security for your files, and the ability to customize your store
  • The file security features can help you protect your digital property by allowing you to put PDF stamps, set download limits, and SSL encryption.
  • Sellfy provides unlimited support.
  • Sellfy provides simple and intuitive tax and VAT configuration settings.
  • Marketing strategies include coupons, email marketing, upselling, tracking pixels, and cart abandonment.

Cons

  • Although the free plan is helpful, but it limits you to only 10 products.
  • Payment plans often require an upgrade if you exceed a certain sales amount per year.
  • The storefront designs are clean, but they're not unique templates for creating a completely different brand image.
  • Sellfy's branding is removed from your hosted product when you upgrade to the $49 per month Business plan.
  • The free plan does not allow for selling digital or subscription products.

Conclusion

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9661. NVIDIA's CEO Shake-Up Exposes a Costly Prediction Market Deadline

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

This week’s PF Weekly found it hard to ignore what is happening at NVIDIA. Jensen Huang resigned, and finance chief Colette Kress took over while the board looks for a permanent CEO. The trade that caught our eye was Kalshi’s “Before Nov 12, 2026” contract.

A Yes share paid $1 only if Huang had left as CEO and his departure had been announced by the end of Wednesday, 11 November, Eastern time. Yes traded as high as 90¢ that night. It paid zero.

At 9:11 p.m. ET on Wednesday, buyers on Kalshi paid about $12,870 for 15,500 Yes shares on that midnight deadline in seven seconds, at prices from 78¢ to 90¢. The price was back near 50¢ within half a minute. By midnight it was down to 1¢. Kalshi’s separate contract on an exit by year-end was still at 83¢.

The final hour was the busiest for the midnight contract. Some 2.38 million contracts changed hands. Open interest, the number of contracts still outstanding, rose from 2.95 million to 4.14 million even as the Yes price fell.

NVIDIA’s SEC filing says the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday, effective immediately. The company announced it at 8:48 a.m. ET on Thursday, after Kalshi’s cutoff. Polymarket’s “by November 12” contract included Thursday, so its Yes shares paid $1.

Kalshi’s two earliest deadlines accounted for 11.24 million of the 19.84 million contracts traded on Huang’s exit, or 57%. On Polymarket, the first two deadlines drew $13.18 million of the $22.73 million in reported volume, or 58%.

On Polymarket, NVIDIA’s price to finish 2026 as the world’s most valuable company fell from 64¢ on 3 November to 22¢ by Wednesday’s stock-market close, then to 11¢ by Thursday’s close. Apple went from about 35¢ to 86¢ over the same stretch. Roughly four-fifths of NVIDIA’s drop in that contract had happened before the resignation announcement. Investors were already questioning how the AI buildout would be financed.

For December 2027, I’d start with the gap in market value. Apple ended Thursday at about $5.16 trillion and NVIDIA at $4.01 trillion. If Apple stays flat, NVIDIA needs to gain about 29% to draw level. If Apple gains 10%, NVIDIA needs about 42%. If Apple loses 10%, NVIDIA needs about 16%. That cushion makes Apple my starting favourite for 2027. Microsoft ended Thursday only about 3% behind NVIDIA, so the race could get tighter from behind as well.

NVIDIA executive Ian Buck led the permanent CEO markets on Kalshi and Polymarket at about 30% in the Friday snapshots we checked. Kalshi put the chance of a permanent appointment being announced at about one in five before 1 January and close to two in three before 1 February. Kress is already running the company, and 17 November will be NVIDIA’s first earnings call with her as interim CEO.

Back in August, NVIDIA guided to $108 billion in quarterly revenue and gave a preliminary outlook for roughly 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which covers most of calendar 2027. I’ll be listening for whether Kress still expects that pace of growth and whether shipments of its new Vera Rubin systems are on schedule.

The succession market gives us a read on who might lead NVIDIA next. Tuesday’s call gives us the first chance to see whether the business is still on course to close the gap with Apple.

#9660. Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

One of the oldest running bug disclosure programs announced it would shorten public disclosure timelines to vendors from 120 days to 30 over the next 14 months.

Google will soon drastically reduce the disclosure deadlines of vulnerabilities prior to publicly disclosing them, and the move has sparked concern among some cybersecurity professionals.

Project Zero, Google's third-party vulnerability remediation program, currently follows what it describes as "90+30" policy: 90 days to remediate a vulnerability and an extra 30-day "soak time" to allow for patch rollout before publicly disclosing the bug. This will no longer be the case. As of the announcement on Nov. 13, Google changed its policy to disclose 90 days after reporting to the vendor. As of Feb. 2, 2027, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 60 days. As of Jan. 3, 2028, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 30 days.

In a blog post outlining the decision, Google's Natalie Silvanovich wrote that while the intention of 90+30 was to encourage faster patching while giving vendors time to deliver patches, "The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Specifically, Silvanovich noted that large language models have enabled threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities much faster in today's AI era.

"A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster," she wrote. "LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior."

Project Zero is not a conventional bug disclosure program. Founded in 2014, the organization was established specifically so Google could help facilitate the safe reporting and disclosure of high-severity, high-impact vulnerabilities found in widely used software and hardware. That said, Project Zero's move reflects a broad inundation of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and where Google goes, the rest of the industry may follow.

As for whether such a thing is good, bad, or necessary for the cybersecurity industry, experts appear to be split.

Disclosure timelines are a key part of the vulnerability ecosystem. When a researcher or firm discovers a vulnerability and submits it to the software developer responsible, a standard timeline is usually designated for the developer to fix the vulnerability; such deadlines are usually 90 or 120 days, but it varies depending on the bug, disclosure policy, and circumstances.

Related:'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

If the software developer ignores the bug report, is slow to address it, or declines to communicate with the researcher, the researcher may choose to disclose the flaw at the end of the disclosure timeline to inform security teams and practitioners of the looming threat. These timelines hold software vendors accountable and encourage them to maintain secure software, but it's not perfect science.

Oftentimes, the researcher and software developer will work together to coordinate a disclosure date so relevant research, patches, and mitigations are ready at the same time. Sometimes, if the bug is especially dangerous or requires more time to fix, the timeline may change and the technical details and proof-of-concept exploits will be held until a later date.

It's worth noting there are no standard requirements between platforms. HackerOne keeps its default disclosure timeline to 30 days, though it's broadly set at the program level by each vendor customer, and many HackerOne programs set longer timelines. Bugcrowd researchers and vendors generally coordinate timelines; program rules again supersede standards.

Related:November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative (which is not a platform but a vendor-agnostic vulnerability disclosure program) uses a standard disclosure timeline of 120 days for responsive vendors that release working patches, and shorter timelines for vulnerabilities that result from faulty patches.

It remains to be seen whether the larger industry will follow Project Zero's lead. Dustin Childs, ZDI's head of threat awareness, calls Google's decision "a bold move to be sure, especially considering the explosion of bug reports coming in thanks to AI assisted discovery."

However, he worries about how shorter timelines may impact remediation quality. "I fear it will lead to patches that don’t fully address the vulnerability. We see that happen at 120 days," Childs says. "We’ll be watching closely to see how this change impacts vendors and researchers alike."

Alex Rice, cofounder, CISO, and CTO at HackerOne, tells Dark Reading that he expects the industry to move in Google's direction, though not necessarily in lockstep. He argues that patch soak time no longer protects defenders, given how quickly attackers can exploit flaws now. And because Project Zero is a disclosure program for vulnerabilities with demonstrated impact and not a bug bounty platform that addresses a broad range of flaws, Google is in a unique position to set aggressive expectations.

"The specifics will still vary by program, severity, and whether a fix is realistic, and platforms like ours will need to support that flexibility," Rice says. "But the direction isn’t in question. Organizations should plan for 30 days as the baseline expectation that will shrink even further."

Between stories from this year about AI models capable of discovering zero-day bugs off of human language prompts and vulnerability coordinators fighting huge spikes in bug reporting volumes the past couple of years, Google's position seems defensible. The tech giant isn't alone in its move either: In January, Anthropic's own coordinated disclosure policy will shorten from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity bugs, and 45 days for all other cases.

But not everyone agrees. Expel principal threat researcher Marcus Hutchins took issue with the move in a post to X, where he noted that 2026 has already seen far more CVEs than 2025. "Sure, there are some vendors who just sit on bugs forever and don't make any effort to patch them. But there's way more overworked & underpaid teams, non-profits, and solo projects who are patching bugs as fast as they physically can," he wrote.

Katie Moussouris, CEO of Luta Security and a pioneer in vulnerability disclosure, largely agrees. As she tells Dark Reading, even AI firms currently struggle to patch the issues they find, leaving volunteers and less resourced firms even further back against the wall. "A deadline doesn't magically manifest a fix."

"Researchers and AI companies are burying maintainers in bug reports and not doing enough to help fix them. This isn't even a matter of model access or token cost. The AI companies themselves can't even close the gap," she says. "Anthropic reports that 629 of the 5,087 vulnerabilities it disclosed have been patched. OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, run with security engineers from Trail of Bits, has written patches for a third of the 2,055 issues it found, and 23% have been accepted upstream."

[Editor's Note: After publication, a Trail of Bits spokesperson told Dark Reading that of the most recent finding of 2,162 issues found, 733 have a patch written, and among those, 506 (or about 69%) have been accepted or merged upstream.]

A Google spokesperson tells Dark Reading that in creating the new policy, the company solicited feedback from the vendors Project Zero reports the most vulnerabilities to, including open source projects.

"The general consensus was that these timelines are achievable, and most open source projects are almost there," the spokesperson says. "Every vulnerability that Project Zero reported against a volunteer-maintained project in 2026 was fixed in 30 days, except for one, which was fixed in 31 days. Open source projects are among the vendors who will need to make the fewest changes to meet our new policy, as they are already doing so well."

While one side of the argument disagrees with the rollout of shorter timelines, the other side sees it as inevitable or necessary to respond to how attackers now use AI to pursue their goals. HackerOne's Rice says that right now, teams are not ready to deal with a 30-day turnaround, but Google's move may offer an opportunity at the boardroom level to convince technology and executive partners that remediation is a shared responsibility.

"If you're a security team struggling to keep up, don't waste time playing the victim. Take this as a gift," he says. "Ask for dedicated engineering capacity for security fixes, pre-agreed remediation SLAs, automated validation and retesting, and the authority to ship mitigations while the full fix is built. The teams that turn this pressure into that conversation will be far ahead of the ones hoping for external relief."

Casey Ellis, founder of Bugcrowd and The disclose.io Project, says this is a necessary evolution, even if it feels aggressive. In the wake of proliferated vulnerability discovery, the timeline shortening "puts productive pressure on response and fix pipelines."

Ellis says he feels the typical targets of Project Zero researchers are in "decent shape," but community norms tend to follow Google's lead on CVE timelines, so the move could carry larger impact.

"My main concern would be companies that maintain safety-critical systems or those that are otherwise logistically difficult to update; a security fix doesn't always end with a patch, and more often than not, it doesn't," he says. "The Project Zero changes will ultimately reveal (and hopefully shrink or close) the readiness gap for many PSIRT teams, products, and hosted service providers, but unless product vendors become proactive about this aspect of vulnerability discovery and disclosure it is likely to be a bumpy ride for some."

This story was updated on Nov. 18, 2026 at 8:47 a.m. ET, with additional context shared by a Trail of Bits spokesperson regarding figures included in the article.

#9658. Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Two AI agents, separately over a five-day period, autonomously tried to access connected applications, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, without account owner permission.

Grok Bots attempted to access corporate applications without their users' approval or knowledge, presenting yet another security challenge for enterprises as AI agents become increasingly autonomous.

Researchers at NewCore identified 31 unprompted attempts by two xAI Grok Bots to access connected corporate applications over a five-day period, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, according to the findings of an investigation published today. In one case, the bot continued making background requests even after its owner had declined offers for recurring check-ins four times.

The requests were not approved and did not reach the underlying corporate data: NewCore had placed a security gateway between the agents and the applications, requiring human approval for each request.

"Over five days, two Grok Bots on NewCore employee accounts made 31 requests to calendar, email, Slack, GitHub and Notion while nobody was talking to them, some with the laptop shut," Ido Hoorvitch, security research team lead at NewCore, wrote in the report.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

One bot repeatedly attempted to retrieve Google Calendar events in the evening, overnight, and the following day, despite there being no active conversation with its owner. In a second case, another bot attempted to access Notion's calendar tools before Google Calendar had even been connected. It continued making requests while its owner's laptop was closed and asleep.

The investigation began as an internal experiment at NewCore, which wanted to understand how autonomous AI agents behave when connected to real corporate systems. The company earlier this year provided employees with enterprise Grok Bot accounts and connected the agents to corporate services, including email, calendars, Notion, and other business applications.

However, NewCore put a handbrake in place: It did not give the agents unrestricted, standing access to company data. Instead, requests had to pass through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway. The gateway sent an approval notification to the employee who owned the account whenever a Grok Bot tried to access an application. If a request was not approved within three minutes, it automatically expired and was denied, Hoorvitch said.

"We did it because we had no way to audit why an agent reaches for data, and until we do, the gate stays closed by default," he wrote. Ultimately, this security control allowed NewCore to observe and reconstruct the bots' background activity.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

The first sign that something was amiss came after an employee used Grok Bot to retrieve their daily calendar, approving the request through the gateway as expected. Later that evening, however, the gateway recorded further calendar access attempts, despite the employee no longer interacting with the bot.

This led investigators to uncover repeated attempts by Grok agents to access corporate applications without any corresponding user interaction. Moreover, when one bot was asked whether it had made the gateway calls, it said it had not, Hoorvitch said. The requests did not appear in the bot's chat history.

"It was telling the truth. … That is the part to sit with," he wrote. "An agent that cannot account for its own actions is not a bug report. It is a finding."

NewCore contacted xAI about its findings and said the company's support team confirmed that the activity was not the result of a software vulnerability or an exploit, but was part of Grok Bot's built-in background check-in functionality.

"These are built-in background check-ins by the primary bot, during a check-in the bot looks at its connected sources, and there is no user or admin setting to turn them off," Hoorvitch wrote, relaying the response from xAI support.

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

According to NewCore, xAI also said that customers seeking to stop the check-ins could send the vendor a list of employee sign-in addresses. NewCore said it had not received an official response from xAI's media team at the time the report was published.

The lack of a user- or administrator-facing setting to disable background check-ins, or to control which connected tools they can use, creates a visibility and governance challenge for security teams. Employees may not know when an AI agent is accessing connected applications, while the agent itself may not retain a record of its server-initiated activity in the chat history visible to its owner.

"The danger is not that the model goes rogue," Hoorvitch explains to Dark Reading. "The concern is that we hand agents standing credentials and then let someone else decide when they act. The owner thinks the bot works when they talk to it. The vendor thinks a helpful bot checks in on its own. The model does what the platform tells it in that turn, not what the owner would have said."

Though "nobody in that chain is malicious," he says, "the result is still a bot reading your inbox at 7:46 a.m. while you are asleep."

The distinction matters because all 31 unattended requests identified by NewCore were read operations, such as retrieving calendar events or searching messages, Hoorvitch explains. None resulted in data being accessed, because the gateway blocked them. However, the same connected tool sets included capabilities to take actions, such as sending email, modifying calendar events, and posting Slack messages. NewCore warned that the same background processes could pose a greater risk if they were to invoke those write-capable tools.

In NewCore's investigation, its MCP gateway blocked all 31 unattended requests. The company argues that organizations need similar independent controls to set and enforce policies on AI agents operating within their systems.

"Put the decision outside the agent," Hoorvitch says. "Route every agent tool call through something you own, like the NewCore MCP Gateway, where the owner's policy decides what goes through and every call is logged whether or not the agent remembers it."

NewCore also recommends that organizations immediately inventory the agents connected to corporate tools, identify which applications and data they can reach, and assign an owner to each. Security teams should review not only approved activity but also requests that were denied or left unanswered, since these can reveal what agents attempt to do without user involvement.

"Most teams cannot answer that today," Hoorvitch says, "and you cannot govern what you cannot list."
